title: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)

guidelineVersions: INTEGRATE (UK ENT Trainee Research Network). Admission avoidance in tonsillitis and peritonsillar abscess (Clinical Otolaryngology, 2021)

related.why: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage: another tonsil/oropharynx ENT emergency

brief.scenario: Ms Aisha Merritt, 24, has severe unilateral throat pain, difficulty swallowing and a muffled voice.
brief.task: Assess the likely diagnosis and explain your initial management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Airway and swallowing first, then the clinical diagnosis, then complications, then management.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating this as simple tonsillitis and sending her home on oral antibiotics without assessing airway risk.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess her airway, hydration and systemic illness first, before confirming the diagnosis."

flow: Ask about drooling and swallowing saliva

grid.label: Airway-first assessment (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Goes straight to naming the diagnosis or starting treatment without first assessing airway, hydration and systemic illness.
grid.pass: Assesses airway, hydration and systemic illness first, before confirming the diagnosis and starting treatment.
grid.high: Explains that a toxic patient unable to swallow saliva needs urgent senior ENT review before anything else is arranged.

grid.label: Clinical diagnosis
grid.fail: Diagnoses simple tonsillitis despite unilateral swelling and trismus, or cannot name the diagnosis.
grid.pass: Recognises this as a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), looking for unilateral peritonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, trismus and muffled voice.
grid.high: Correlates the examination with the history rather than assuming every case of uvular deviation is a quinsy, and considers alternative causes of a similar picture.

grid.label: Targeted airway-risk questions
grid.fail: Does not ask specifically about drooling, breathing difficulty or the ability to swallow saliva.
grid.pass: Specifically asks about drooling, breathing difficulty and inability to swallow saliva, because these increase concern about significant upper-airway disease.
grid.high: Uses the answers to these questions to decide how urgently to escalate, rather than asking them as a checklist.

grid.label: Complications
grid.fail: Names no complication beyond "it could get worse", or does not consider deep neck-space infection.
grid.pass: Considers deep neck-space infection and dehydration as complications, and recognises trismus can make examination and drainage difficult.
grid.high: Explains that airway compromise or deep neck-space spread turns this into an airway emergency requiring urgent specialist management.

grid.label: Management and escalation (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Gives oral antibiotics alone and discharges her, or attempts drainage without considering the airway.
grid.pass: Gives analgesia and appropriate antimicrobial treatment, assesses for aspiration or drainage depending on severity and response, and involves ENT.
grid.high: States that airway compromise or deep neck-space infection escalates this to an airway emergency needing urgent specialist management, not routine ENT referral.

failures.move: Deciding management before assessing airway, hydration and systemic illness.
failures.consequence: A deteriorating airway or systemic sepsis can be missed until it becomes an emergency.

failures.move: Attempting drainage or examination (for example with a tongue depressor) without considering the airway first.
failures.consequence: Can precipitate airway obstruction or bleeding in a patient with trismus and a compromised airway.

failures.move: Treating with oral antibiotics alone and discharging home.
failures.consequence: Untreated or undertreated abscess can progress to deep neck-space infection or airway compromise.

failures.move: Not asking about drooling or the ability to swallow saliva.
failures.consequence: A key marker of significant upper-airway disease is missed, delaying escalation.

knowledge.fact: Quinsy presents with unilateral peritonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, trismus, muffled voice and difficulty swallowing.
The INTEGRATE audit found that ability to swallow fluids or medication was the key triage and discharge criterion for tonsillitis and peritonsillar abscess admissions.
Management is analgesia and antimicrobial treatment, with aspiration or drainage depending on severity and response, and ENT involvement.
Airway compromise or deep neck-space infection makes this an airway emergency needing urgent specialist management.

recall.think: Airway compromise from deep neck-space spread.
recall.say: "This looks like a quinsy — assessing airway, hydration and systemic illness first."

Involve ENT; escalate if airway is threatened

recall.finish: Aspiration or surgical drainage under specialist care, with urgent escalation if the airway is threatened.

partner.opening: Ms Aisha Merritt, 24, has severe unilateral throat pain, difficulty swallowing and a muffled voice. "Assess the likely diagnosis and explain your initial management."

reveals.finding: She is drooling slightly and finds it hard to swallow her own saliva.
Unilateral peritonsillar swelling with contralateral uvular deviation and trismus limiting mouth opening.
She is febrile and tachycardic but able to protect her airway at present.

push.question: Is every sore throat with uvular deviation a quinsy?
push.expect: No — correlate the examination with the history and consider other causes.

push.question: What is your first priority?
push.expect: Airway assessment and recognition of severe systemic illness before confirming the diagnosis.

push.question: Why does trismus matter for your plan?
push.expect: It can make both examination and drainage more difficult, so this is planned for in advance.

curveballs.prompt: She becomes unable to swallow her own saliva and starts drooling more.
curveballs.safeAnswer: This is a marker of significant upper-airway disease — escalate for urgent senior ENT review.

curveballs.prompt: A nurse asks if you can just prescribe oral antibiotics and send her home.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — assess for aspiration or drainage and involve ENT; oral antibiotics alone are not sufficient here.

curveballs.prompt: She develops increasing neck swelling beyond the tonsillar area.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider deep neck-space spread and escalate urgently rather than treating this as simple quinsy.
